articles.title: Bank stopped widow from accessing matured FDs; consumer panel orders Rs 13.87 lakh payment
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: A Kerala district consumer commission has directed a cooperative bank to pay Rs 13.87 lakh to a depositor after it restricted her withdrawa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Kerala district consumer commission has directed a cooperative bank to pay Rs 13.87 lakh to a depositor after it restricted her withdrawals from her savings account despite her fixed deposit hit maturity. The commission also awarded Rs 25,000 compensation and Rs 3,000 litigation costs in an order passed on September 17, 2026.Why did the depositor approach the consumer commission?According to the commission order, the woman had four fixed deposits with the Kandala Sahakarana Sangham Cooperative Bank. After the deposits matured, their proceeds were transferred to her savings account with the bank.The woman initially had Rs 7.44 lakh credited to her account after two fixed deposits were closed. However, the bank allowed her to withdraw only Rs 50,000 and did not release the remaining amount.She later sought the money for her mother's medical treatment and also to repay arrears on a gold loan. Two more fixed deposits of Rs 4 lakh each were subsequently transferred to her savings account. The commission recorded that Rs 13.87 lakh remained in the account as on May 15, 2023.However, the bank argued that withdrawals had been restricted after an inquiry under the Kerala Cooperative Societies Act found irregularities. It said the Registrar of Cooperative Societies had directed it to disburse deposits according to a priority list prepared by a committee.Why did the commission hold the bank responsible?The bench comprising President P V Jayarajan along with members Preetha G Nair and Viju V R held that the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides an additional remedy and therefore the complaint could be heard despite the bank's objection based on the Kerala Cooperative Societies Act.The commission observed that the bank had admitted the fixed deposits, their maturity and transfer of the money into the woman's savings account. The commission said the bank's internal inquiry could not justify delaying the payment.“The enquiry under section 65 of Kerala Co operative Societies Act against the directors and staff of the bank and the consequential departmental directions if any to the opposite party bank cannot be attributed as a justifiable reason for the delay in disbursing the amount deposited by the 2nd complainant with the opposite party bank,” the commission further observed.The commission then noted that the woman was a widow and had claimed the money in the bank was her only source of income.“The second complainant made the deposits in good faith with an expectation that the said amount will be available to her from the opposite party bank as and when any need arises to her. It is important to note that the responsibility of the opposite party bank to ensure that its consumer is satisfied with its services and the deposit is made available to her when she raised the demand for the same,” the bench added.The commission found that the bank had not produced documents supporting its claims about the Section 65 inquiry or the directions allegedly restricting withdrawals.“From the available evidence before this commission, we find that there is deficiency in service and unfair trade practice on the part of the opposite parties. It is also evident from the evidence adduced by the complainant that the complainant has suffered mental agony and financial loss due to the act of the opposite parties,” it added.The commission allowed the complaint and held the bank and its branch jointly and severally liable.It directed them to pay Rs 13,87,408 to the depositor with 9 percent annual interest from February 22, 2023, the date of filing the complaint. It also ordered Rs 25,000 compensation and Rs 3,000 towards litigation costs.The amount was directed to be paid within 30 days of receipt of the order. If the payment is delayed, the Rs 13.87 lakh amount and compensation will carry 9 percent annual interest from the date of the order until realisation.

articles.title: A Pennsylvania flea-market buyer paid $4 for a framed painting; hidden behind it was a rare 1776 Declaration of Independence copy worth $8.14 million
articles.summary: US News: A $4 flea-market purchase in Pennsylvania turned into one of the most remarkable discoveries in American history. In 1989, a man bought a framed paint.
articles.body: A $4 flea-market purchase in Pennsylvania turned into one of the most remarkable discoveries in American history. In 1989, a man bought a framed painting mainly because he wanted the frame. When he later took it apart, he found a folded document hidden behind the canvas. The paper appeared to be a copy of the Declaration of Independence, but its true importance was not immediately understood. Years later, experts identified it as one of the rare surviving copies from the document’s first printing, eventually leading to an $8.14 million sale in 2000.$4 flea-market painting revealed a Declaration of Independence copyThe discovery began at a flea market in Adamstown, Pennsylvania, in 1989. According to HISTORY, the buyer paid just $4 for a framed painting and was primarily interested in making use of its frame. The painting itself was old and torn, and once he took it apart at home, the frame turned out to be unusable.Behind the canvas, however, was something far more significant. A folded sheet of paper had been tucked away inside the frame. The buyer recognised it as the Declaration of Independence but initially believed it was simply a reproduction with little monetary value. Antiques and the Arts reported that he kept the document before eventually being persuaded by a friend to have it examined by Sotheby’s.The discovery was not immediately treated as a major historical find. For several years, the sheet remained with its new owner while its real identity was still unknown.The document came from the first printing in 1776The significance of the paper became clear when Sotheby’s examined it. The document was identified as one of the copies produced by Philadelphia printer John Dunlap on the night of July 4, 1776, shortly after the Declaration was adopted.According to CBS News, Dunlap produced hundreds of copies and sent them to the 13 colonies so that news of independence could be circulated. Only 25 of those copies were known to survive. The copy found behind the painting was therefore not a later reproduction but an exceptionally rare surviving example from the first printing.Antiques and the Arts reported that of the only 25 surviving copies, just 4 were held by private collectors at the time. Most of the others were in museums and public institutions.One small detail also helped reveal the circumstances of its printing. HISTORY reported that the ink had still been wet when the sheet was printed, leaving the first line of the Declaration appearing in reverse at the bottom of the page. It was a physical trace of the hurried printing process surrounding one of the most important documents in American history.Sotheby’s authentication changed the value of the discoveryThe document was taken to Sotheby’s for a professional evaluation several years after it was found. David Redden, then Sotheby’s executive vice president, travelled to Pennsylvania to authenticate it.Antiques and the Arts reported that Redden immediately recognised that the document was genuine and described its condition as exceptionally impressive. The authentication transformed what had seemed to be an ordinary piece of paper into a rare historical object with enormous value.The document eventually entered the auction world. CBS News reported that Sotheby’s had sold it in 1991 for $2.4 million to Visual Equities, a fine-art investment firm based in Atlanta. It was offered again in 1993 but failed to sell at auction.Its journey did not end there. By 2000, the document was back on the market, where its value would rise dramatically.The auction held in 2000 pushed the price to $8.14 millionThe final stage of the story came in June 2000, when television producer Norman Lear and internet entrepreneur David Hayden bought the Declaration of Independence copy through Sotheby’s.CBS News reported that bidding began at $4 million. Lear and Hayden competed against another prospective buyer, placing 29 separate bids before the bidding reached $7.4 million. After Sotheby’s commission was added, the final price came to $8.14 million.Antiques and the Arts reported that the bidding had been expected to settle at around $6 million, but a late burst of competition pushed the final price beyond $8 million. The sale established a new record for an American historical document at the time.Norman Lear planned to take the historic document across AmericaLear and Hayden did not describe their purchase simply as a private collecting opportunity. CBS News reported that they planned to put the Declaration on a national tour, allowing people in different parts of the United States to see the document.Antiques and the Arts also reported that the pair intended to loan the Declaration to People for the American Way Foundation, an organisation founded by Lear. Their stated aim was to make the document accessible to a much wider public instead of keeping it solely in a private collection.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'No change in President Trump's position': UK to review Chagos Islands deal with Mauritius
articles.summary: UK News: The UK is \"reviewing\" its Chagos Islands deal with Mauritius, British defence secretary Wes Streeting said on Wednesday, saying the decision was taken.
articles.body: The UK is "reviewing" its Chagos Islands deal with Mauritius, British defence secretary Wes Streeting said on Wednesday, saying the decision was taken because the United States "does not support" the agreement.His remarks came a day after US President Donald Trump, who initially gave his approval to the deal but later reversed his decision, called it "terrible" during his first face-to-face meeting with the UK's new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, at the UN General Assembly in New York City.The UK had already paused the Chagos Islands agreement in April following Trump's change in stance."What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new, but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," Streeting told the BBC, referring to Trump's remarks during the Burnham meeting."So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it," the defence secretary added.According to Streeting, the focus now would be on securing a "long-term certainty" for a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the Chagos archipelago. The base shares its name with the island.Under the original agreement, signed in May 2025 after Trump's approval the previous month, the UK would cede sovereignty of the archipelago to Mauritius and pay an average of £101 million ($136 million) per year to lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, owing to its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.However, Trump's U-turn in January led to the deal being paused. In addition, a final draft of the bill to transfer sovereignty of the islands had not passed the UK Parliament, as then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to about £35 billion, after adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.Mauritius argues that it was "illegally" forced to give away the Chagos Islands in 1965 as a condition for gaining independence from Britain.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tigray forces launch offensive against Ethiopian government
articles.summary: Tigray People’s Liberation Front seizes control of airports, targets government positions in Afar and Amhara regions.
articles.body:
Tigrayan rebels have seized control of airports in the Tigray region in northern Ethiopia and launched an offensive against federal forces in the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) has “launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara”, Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said in a post on his X account on Wednesday.

“It has taken over federally controlled airports in Tigray leading to the suspension of flights to and from Tigray. The TPLF politico-military leadership has obviously taken irresponsibility to new heights,” said Reda, a former TPLF leader who fell out with the party and joined the federal government.

The Tigray regional government, however, said it was countering an “invasion” by federal forces.

In a statement posted on Facebook, it accused federal troops of “intensive bombardments” on Tuesday involving “aircraft, drones, and artillery”.

“The Tigray army has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion launched against us, and has entered into a defensive battle,” the statement added.

Clashes were under way in various parts of Afar, including Abala and Berahle, amid reports of shelling along the border with Amhara, and an Al Jazeera correspondent reported significant military build-ups by various parties in the border areas.

The development comes after the TPLF announced on Sunday that it had allied with six other armed groups across Ethiopia to overthrow Abiy’s government.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined after Abiy took office, triggering a devastating civil war from 2020 to 2022. The conflict killed about 600,000 people, according to estimates by the African Union, before the Pretoria Peace Agreement ended hostilities.

The region has still not recovered. About one million people remain displaced, and parts of the peace agreement are unfulfilled. An uneasy calm held until late 2025 when clashes resumed, and a further escalation in recent months has raised fears of a return to all-out war.

Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, said with the peace agreement broken down, the situation has turned very dangerous.

“The TPLF has joined with other rebel groups to say that they are going to overthrow and topple the current regime, which is something very close to a declaration of war,” Boswell told Al Jazeera.

“We’ve seen an ongoing and escalating drone campaign by the federal government against the TPLF, and then you’ve seen quite an escalation over the past day. So if we’re not all the way back into something like a full war, we are very, very close,” he said.

He also noted that with Eritrea allying itself with the TPLF, the issue threatens to become a regional one. Ethiopia’s federal government and its allies in Eritrea fought the TPLF together in the civil war, but now Ethiopia’s federal government accuses those same former allies of supporting the TPLF.

“Eritrea is also quite close, for instance, with the Sudanese army, and relations between Ethiopia and the Sudanese army have also been deteriorating,” Boswell said, adding that Ethiopia is also getting more involved in the Sudan war essentially against the Sudanese, at least along its border.

“So this is all becoming one big regional mess, and it could get very, very ugly if we don’t see de-escalation.”

articles.title: Bringing this popular drink to a job interview could hurt your chances, experts warn
articles.summary: An etiquette expert warns that bringing iced coffee or other beverages to a job interview signals casualness and says the professionalism rule applies to all ages.
articles.body: A cup of coffee might be a daily ritual for most Americans, but some career and etiquette experts say bringing one into a job interview could hurt your chances of getting hired. A viral debate has erupted over whether an iced coffee sends the wrong message to hiring managers or if it's simply part of a busy day. Caitlin Wehniainen, a Florida-based corporate recruiter with 16 years of experience recruiting for Fortune 500 companies, sparked the conversation with a video in which she called out Gen Z job candidates for going to interviews with a coffee in hand. CAN YOU BRING A BIRTHDAY CAKE TO A RESTAURANT? VIRAL PIZZERIA DISPUTE REVEALS THE RULES "When you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte, it is perceived — from my opinion and a hiring standpoint — that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day," she said in a recent TikTok video that has amassed more than 17,000 likes and 5,000 comments. "It looks like you went to Target, went to Starbucks, and now you're stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing." It looks "a little too casual," Wehniainen added. "Save that for well before the interview or after the interview. Go and get one. But don’t like waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn’t have time to finish your coffee beforehand." Social media users flooded the comment section, with many agreeing that it is "diabolical" to bring a wet cup dripping with condensation and rattling with ice into the room. WHY RESTAURANT SERVERS CLEAR YOUR PLATE BEFORE EVERYONE FINISHES EATING "That generation has lost the art of professionalism," one TikToker commented. The viral coffee debate joins a growing list of workplace faux pas involving Gen Z, including bringing parents to sit in on interviews, as Fox News Digital previously reported. But others stood up for candidates getting their caffeine fix during an interview. GEN Z TURNS ON CLASSIC SNACKS, FORCING MAJOR GROCERY SHAKE-UP: 'THEY DON'T TRUST THEM' "An interview IS just a stop in my day," one woman said on TikTok. "It's not my whole day." "Are you expecting my whole day to revolve around a 30 min meeting," someone else said. "If showing up with a beverage like a coffee is an issue … that's not a company that I want to work for." A man who said he was also a recruiter offered another point of view: "If you can show up early or on time with the iced coffee you're already showing good time management." COMMUNAL DINING MAKES GEN Z COMEBACK, BUT OLDER GUESTS PUSH BACK ON 'CHAOTIC' TREND Others pointed to the already challenging job market. "If showing up with a beverage like a coffee is an issue … that's not a company that I want to work for," someone commented on TikTok. Others said it's more nuanced. One TikToker noted that, since Wehniainen recruits for Fortune 500 companies, interviews and candidates tend to be more "buttoned up," but that won't be the case everywhere. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Diane Gottsman, a national etiquette expert and the owner of the Protocol School of Texas, said it's therefore best to "err on the side of caution." "Perception is everything," Gottsman told Fox News Digital. "What one person may think is fine, another person may not." "I think bringing in that cup of iced coffee signals both a distraction, a level of comfort and casualness that may not be there," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We're not pointing the finger only at a certain generation," Gottsman added, noting that workers of all ages make similar etiquette mistakes. Beyond coffee, Gottsman said candidates should avoid other distractions or unprofessional impressions by putting away their phones, skipping overpowering fragrances, removing sunglasses from the tops of their heads and avoiding chewing gum. As distracting as an iced latte can be during an in-person job interview, there's another item that can irk hiring managers: the cellphone. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "One job candidate not only placed her cellphone face up on the conference room table during our interview, she also repeatedly leaned over to read incoming texts and even began texting as well while I was speaking to her," said one New York-based manager. The interview ended early. The candidate was not hired. "After your job interview, why not treat yourself to your favorite iced coffee drink as a treat for a job well done?" If an interviewer offers coffee or water, Gottsman said, it's perfectly acceptable to accept — but don't ask for more than what was offered. And if candidates need a drink of water from a bottle tucked away in a bag, she recommends politely asking before taking a sip. Gottsman also noted that interviews are a two-way street. While employers are evaluating candidates, applicants should also be deciding whether a company's culture and expectations are the right fit for them. She and Wehniainen agree that there is a time and place for everything. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "After your job interview, why not treat yourself to your favorite iced coffee drink as a treat for a job well done?" Gottsman added.

articles.title: Once part of the historic Wiborg Estate, Lee Radziwill's East Hampton home sold for $16.2M in 2001; rebuilt after a 2013 fire, 'Dune Cottage' was listed for $120M before selling for $72M
articles.summary: News News: The ‘Dune Cottage’, which was once part of the historic Wiborg Estate and later owned by Lee Radziwill, has changed hands for $72 million. The sale of.
articles.body: The ‘Dune Cottage’, which was once part of the historic Wiborg Estate and later owned by Lee Radziwill, has changed hands for $72 million. The sale of the 3.6-acre oceanfront compound in East Hampton closed in March this year, making it the largest known home sale in the Hamptons in 2026, Hamptons Coastal reported.The estate at 43 East Dune Lane entered the market in 2024, with an asking price of $120 million. After sitting on the market for seven weeks, it received a $25 million discount, reflecting the pricing pressure faced even by trophy properties. Many prospective buyers approached, and the deal was closed for $72 million.Terry Cohen of Compass, along with Hedgerow Exclusive Properties and Chris Covert and Adam Modlin of Modlin Group Hamptons, represented the sellers. The buyer’s identity remains undisclosed.The property’s historyThe home at 43 East Dune Lane is a 3.6-acre oceanfront estate with 225 feet of direct Atlantic Ocean frontage and a rebuilt main residence. Designed in 1910 by renowned architect Grosvenor Atterbury, the residence was commissioned as part of an 80-acre estate owned by Frank Wiborg, an ink-manufacturing magnate. Nearby Wiborg's Beach is named after him. Sara Murphy, Wiborg's daughter, inherited the property later, and it became a central figure in the Jazz Age social scene. She hosted many legendary gatherings attended by prominent artists and writers.Later, in 1941, the mansion was demolished, as it became too expensive to maintain during wartime. The smaller ‘cottage’ survived, and in the late 1980s, socialite Lee Radziwill, sister of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, and her then-husband, Herbert Ross, bought the property for $6.2 million. In 1999, the property grabbed national attention after comedian Jerry Seinfeld signed a $19 million contract to purchase it. But the deal never went through, as Radziwill and Ross backed out at the last moment. This decision came at a huge cost.In 2001, Ann Tenenbaum and her husband, Thomas H. Lee, acquired the estate for $16.2 million. Tenenbaum, a venture-capital investor and philanthropist, and private-equity titan Lee gave the cottage a substantial renovation after buying it. The home underwent another meticulous reconstruction following a destructive fire in 2013. The 2016 rebuild transformed the 11,000-square-foot main residence while still honouring Atterbury's original 1910 design aesthetic.The couple lived in the Hamptons for 20 years. After Lee's death in 2023, Tenenbaum wanted to sell it. Talking to the Wall Street Journal, Tenenbaum said she wanted to put her Hamptons days behind her. “It was very much his place. I loved having family and friends around. I just didn’t love the Hamptons,” she told the outlet.She added, “I’m done with the Hamptons. Now it’s my time to go be in Santa Fe or Malibu or Greece. I don’t know… maybe I want to be a gypsy for a little bit.”What the buyer getsThe main house covers more than 11,000 square feet, with eight bedrooms, 10 baths, and two half baths. Recrafted by master builder Ben Krupinski with tasteful additions to key living areas, the Hamptons home also has a detached two-bedroom guest cottage, a heated oceanside pool, and a tennis court distributed across 225 feet of direct Atlantic frontage.There is a tunnel running from the pool to the lower level, which was engineered to prevent sand from entering living spaces. The full lower level houses a screening room, gym, wellness centre, and private grotto. The main living room, 15 feet high, opens to oceanside terracing overlooking the Atlantic.Dune Cottage hit the market for $120 million, assuming buyers would pay premium multiples for oceanfront acreage, historical provenance, and a complete modern rebuild. But the market didn't quite go with it. It was sold for $72 million, which is a 40 per cent reduction, one of the steeper discounts in Hamptons ultra-luxury sales. The property sat for weeks before the price dropped to $95 million, then dropped again when a buyer finally materialised at $72 million. According to the listing agents, that’s still a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to own one of the most exceptional and historically significant properties in the Hamptons.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Off sick? You need to phone your boss, back-to-work adviser says
articles.summary: Relying on text and email means sick workers disengaged and were less likely to work again, says Sir Charlie Mayfield.
articles.body:
People off sick from work should keep in phone contact with their boss, government-appointed back-to-work expert Sir Charlie Mayfield has said.

Getting bosses and workers to have a conversation, rather than simply exchanging emails and sicknotes, could help get people back into work, Sir Charlie, who is leading the Keep Britain Working taskforce, said.

His latest report said health-related economic inactivity was costing Britain around £210bn a year in benefit payments and lost output.

Talking on the phone was just "one piece of the jigsaw" he said on Wednesday.

The report calls for more workplace support for people with health conditions and disabilities and the establishment of a Workplace Health System alongside the NHS.

But improving communication was also a way to "rehumanise" the workplace and help prevent people dropping out of work altogether, Sir Charlie said.

The report does not suggest that someone struck down by flu needs to croak through their symptoms over the phone or that bosses need to provide down-the-line sickbed sympathy if an employee is off with food poisoning.

"I'm not worried about a day here and a day there. It is more about longer term issues," Sir Charlie told the BBC's Today Programme.

But he said Britain was doing a "poor job" of handling sickness in the workplace, leading to more people becoming disengaged and dropping out altogether.

"I have met so many people who have said to me, 'You know, I was signed off sick and I was off sick for a month, two months, three months, and I had almost no contact with my employer'," Sir Charlie said.

Around 300,000 people leave work every year with a health condition, much of which is preventable, the report said.

Sir Charlie said employees sometimes feared talking about long-term health issues with their employer.

"But the fear is also felt by employers as well because they're afraid of causing offence or creating a complaint or a grievance," he added.

Fear on both sides can create a distance and lack of understanding, he warned, with longer absences making it much more likely a worker will drop out of the labour force altogether.

"If you can keep more people in work, there's a massive opportunity for us to add billions to the economy and, frankly, to people's livelihoods," Sir Charlie said.

"To get that, though, you need to have people talking to each other, and you've got to more actively manage sickness and ill health in the workplace."

Employers need to do more, he said, and employees need to engage with it.

Other ways for bosses to support staff include ensuring access to treatments such as physiotherapy and talking therapies, he said.

articles.summary: Trump tells world leaders he could “annihilate” Iran.
articles.body: Trump tells world leaders he could “annihilate” Iran. ICE under scrutiny again after incidents in Texas and Illinois. And authorities investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students that could be linked to “gas station drug” kratom. Here’s what to know today. Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to “annihilate” Iran, called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and suggested a name change for AI, in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The wide-ranging speech came ahead of several anticipated meetings on the sidelines with world leaders, including his first with Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, since the administration’s capture of Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. Today, Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington, D.C., to meet with Trump to talk trade, Taiwan and AI. On Iran, Trump said the Islamic Republic could make a deal with the U.S. that would allow it to rebuild but predicted a deal won’t happen until after November’s midterm elections. Most important, Trump said to applause, is ensuring that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.” Less than a minute into his remarks, Trump called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and pointed to his administration’s tax policy and stock market records. But gas prices remain high at an average of $4.47 per gallon and diesel prices are currently over $6. Trump declined to endorse guardrails on AI but pushed to change its name to “superintelligence.” He also touted his record on immigration, tying his crackdown on the southern border to a drop in violent crime in the United States. Read the recap of Trump’s speech. Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’ The Department of Justice said in a court filing late yesterday that the president has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of an emergency hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access. The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing. The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier yesterday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes, and citing a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” The letters cite stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia. Here’s what else we know. Analysis: The Trump administration now finds itself defending the media ban as some Republican candidates in competitive races are increasingly distancing themselves from the president. More politics news: The Trump administration removed roughly 750,000 people from their Affordable Care Act plans, claiming that many were receiving subsidies they didn’t qualify for. Health care has become a vulnerable topic for Republicans in the midterms — but they’re still leaning in, even though they don’t expect to win on the issue. For subscribers: Florida’s Trump-endorsed GOP nominee for governor, Byron Donalds, scrubbed nearly every mention of the president from his website.The fight over Missouri’s congressional map returned to the U.S. Supreme Court for a third time late yesterday, after an appeals court ordered the revival of new districts backed by Trump. ICE encounters in Texas and Illinois under scrutiny The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas, wasn’t wearing a body camera during the shooting on Sunday, two Department of Homeland Security sources said. It wasn’t clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera even though another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle wore one, the sources said. An off-duty Austin police officer also captured part of the encounter. Here’s what the Austin police video shows. Deportation proceedings against the man, 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, were blocked yesterday in an emergency order, his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said. Meanwhile, police in Evanston, Illinois, are investigating an incident in which a man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him. An ICE agent told Evanston police that he was attempting “identify a man who resembled a person they were seeking,” but the man refused to provide identification and “resisted detention.” ICE released the man after they learned he was a U.S. citizen and not the person they were seeking. See video from the incident. ‘Gas station drug’ found at locations where two Ole Miss students were discovered dead Authorities in Mississippi are warning the public to avoid kratom and other medications or substances that aren’t from a trusted source after two University of Mississippi students were found dead this week. Packaged kratom was found during the separate death investigations, though authorities said they have not confirmed whether it or any other substance was a contributing factor in the deaths. Both Ole Miss students were found dead Monday — one on campus and the other in the city of Oxford, Mayor Robyn Tannehill said. Neither student has been publicly identified. Kratom has gained popularity as an unapproved treatment for pain, anxiety and drug dependence. It’s banned in Oxford but can still be obtained in surrounding cities. It is sometimes sold at gas stations or online. Here’s what else we know. Staff Pick: Inside the church scandal that became a TikTok obsession Last month, Vicky Hernandez went viral on TikTok for her allegations that her husband had an affair with one of her closest friends, and she’d been preoccupied with the fallout. But viewers quickly questioned her framing of the relationship and hurled allegations against her husband to the point that she deleted all but one of her videos. I began digging into what actually happened. Over the last three weeks, I spoke with more than half a dozen former Trinity United Presbyterian Church members, reviewed court filings and internal church records and looked back at years of online posts to piece together a saga that was far more complicated than the viral videos suggested. What emerged was a yearslong conflict and competing accounts of the same events to create a story examining how an insular church controversy in Southern California became one of TikTok’s most closely followed dramas — and what gets lost when deeply personal allegations unfold before an audience of millions. — Pilar Melendez, breaking news editor Read All About It The Supreme Court declined to intervene in a custody battle involving a surrogate who gave birth despite the newborn’s biological parents asking her to get an abortion after a heart defect was discovered. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The "UP ke ladke" bonhomie is beginning to look less like a united front and more like a contest for the upper hand, with Congress and Samajwadi Party leaders trading jabs over who can take on the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. With the 2027 assembly election approaching, are cracks emerging in the INDIA bloc's battle plan against Yogi Adityanath's BJP?Iqra Hasan’s remarks trigger Congress pushbackSP MP Iqra Hasan set off the latest bout of sparring by saying Congress "can't achieve much on its own" and projecting party boss and former CM Akhilesh Yadav as the only leader capable of defeating the BJP in Uttar Pradesh.Her remarks drew a quick response from the Congress, with party leaders pushing back against the suggestion that the SP could take on the BJP by itself.Congress MP Imran Masood said, "She (Iqra Hasan) also cannot do it alone. What is the problem with that? Iqra is our child. She is like our niece.""People from the Trinamool Congress were also saying a lot. Look at what happened in Bengal. Let us move together, and we will remain in peace," he added with a reference to Mamata-led TMC's big defeat in Bengal after contesting solo.Congress leader Udit Raj pointed to the SP's performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election while questioning Iqra's claim."That may be her (Iqra Hasan's) own statement, but we can understand this through an example: when the alliance was formed in 2024, the Samajwadi Party won 36 seats. What was its performance before that? The Samajwadi Party had only six MPs in 2019. So, in politics, one plus one does not always make two; one plus one can make eleven. Therefore, I think she should correct her understanding," Udit Raj told IANS.BJP joins SP-Congress war of wordsThe saffron party, meanwhile, was quick to weigh in on the disagreement. Uttar Pradesh BJP vice-president Neeraj Singh said, "Congress will not be able to achieve anything on its own across the country. And even if it forms an alliance with the Samajwadi Party or any other party in Uttar Pradesh, the people of Uttar Pradesh have already formed an alliance in their hearts with the BJP government..."Iqra, who made the remarks on Monday, had said, "It is an absolutely foolish statement. I think that if there is anyone in Uttar Pradesh who can defeat the BJP, it is only Akhilesh Yadav. Congress will not be able to do anything on its own. If the alliance remains, it will be very good; if it does not, it is a loss for them (Congress), not for us."SP-Cong face a new test: Who gets how many seats?The "UP ke ladke" chemistry that helped Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav pull off a striking upset in the 2024 Lok Sabha election has yet to turn into a clear seat-sharing formula for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.The two leaders have continued to share the stage on occasions, including protest for students, maintaining a public show of camaraderie. But behind that familiar chemistry, the alliance arithmetic is still taking shape.There has been no concrete discussion on how the 403 assembly seats could be divided between Congress and the Samajwadi Party.How 2024 ‘UP ke ladke’ formula workedTheir partnership took shape months before the 2024 Lok Sabha election, and the results that followed gave the alliance a strong political imprint.The SP contested 62 of the state's 80 Lok Sabha seats and won 37, including Faizabad, the constituency covering Ayodhya. Congress fought 17 seats and won six. Akhilesh's party emerged as the largest opposition force in the state, and second largest in country, while Congress revived its presence with six seats.Ayodhya loss added to BJP’s UP setbackThe result also had a powerful political backdrop. Uttar Pradesh is the home turf of chief minister Yogi Adityanath and the parliamentary constituency of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The BJP had also invested enormous political capital in Ayodhya, where the Ram temple consecration took place in January 2024 in the presence of PM Modi and RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat.Yet, months later, the BJP lost the Faizabad seat to the SP.The result turned Rahul and Akhilesh into the "UP ke ladke" of the 2024 campaign, a political pairing that seemed to have found the right formula for the state's electorate. But Congress has not made a similar formal commitment. The party has not yet released a formal candidate list.SP strategists say the early exercise is deliberate, giving prospective candidates time to prepare their constituencies, build networks and hit the ground running once the campaign begins.The strategy is not entirely new. Political observers point out that the SP followed a similar approach before the 2022 assembly and 2024 Lok Sabha elections, beginning the candidate-selection process well ahead of polling but releasing the actual lists only a few months before the election.Congress prepares for all 403 seats tooCongress, meanwhile, has indicated that it is preparing to contest all 403 seats. That ambition could make the eventual negotiatins with the SP considerably more interesting.Owaisi offer adds another variableAnd there is another piece on the chessboard. AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi has made an open offer to Akhilesh, potentially bringing another party into the opposition's seat-sharing calculations.If the SP chooses to engage with Owaisi, the equation could become even more complicated for an alliance that has so far largely revolved around SP and Congress.What happened in 2022 assembly pollsThe Lok Sabha 2024 friendship was a renewed one. articles.title: Salva Kiir: South Sudan president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections
articles.summary: South Sudan has not held elections since independence in 2011 - polls have twice been postponed.
articles.body:
South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011.

The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times.

Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments.

Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason.

Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men.

Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections.

Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city.

A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday.

UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored.

South Sudan's leader sacks aides after dead man appointed

Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng.

Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m.

In June, the main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, warned people not to take part in poll preparations.

"Anyone coming to register voters and campaign in territories controlled by the mighty SPLM-IO, you will be a prisoner of war," Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairperson of the group, said in a post on Facebook.

The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase".

It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence.

The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027.

articles.title: Netanyahu calls Macron's West Bank comments in UN speech 'grotesque'
articles.summary: Israel's PM denounces the French president after he appeared to downplay Hamas's activities in the occupied territory.
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly.

"Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter.

Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day".

There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation".

The source told the Jerusalem Post that the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sévi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank."

Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire

"Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?"

After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering."

"On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank.

"Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria."

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality".

Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said.

Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it.

The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

The settlements are illegal under international law.

articles.title: Watch: Apache firepower joins US war machines during India-US drill Yudh Abhyas
articles.summary: News News: Apache attack helicopters of the Indian Army have joined Indian and US troops for Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, adding an aviation dimension to the ongoi.
articles.body: Apache attack helicopters of the Indian Army have joined Indian and US troops for Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, adding an aviation dimension to the ongoing bilateral drills at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan.The 22nd edition of the exercise is being held simultaneously at Auli in Uttarakhand and the firing range in Rajasthan, with around 600 personnel from each side, including soldiers from the US Army's 11th Airborne Division, taking part.The Apache's participation comes as the Army continues to build up its attack helicopter fleet. It has so far inducted six AH-64E helicopters, which operate out of Jodhpur under the 451 Army Aviation Squadron. During the exercise, the Apache demonstrated rapid target acquisition and precision-strike capabilities, using its sensors, fire-control systems and real-time data links to quickly turn battlefield intelligence into action.First introduced into the US Army in 1986, the Apache has seen combat from Panama to Iraq and Kosovo and remains one of the most capable attack helicopters in service. Powered by twin engines, it can reach speeds of up to 365 kmph. The helicopter was inducted into the Indian Army in July last year and has already been tested in demanding operational conditions. The Indian Air Force's Apache fleet, for instance, was deployed at high altitudes in Eastern Ladakh during the standoff with China.The drills cover a wide spectrum of operations, ranging from a brigade-level command post exercise and expert-level academic discussions to mountain warfare and cold-weather training at Auli, as well as counter-unmanned aircraft system training.Live-fire activity at the Mahajan range includes the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, Stinger missiles and the Mobile Low, Slow, Small Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System (MLIDS). The Apache deployment is focused on joint mission planning, battlefield coordination and precision engagement between attack aviation and ground forces. The drills are intended to help the two armies refine common procedures and communication in a realistic operational environment.Officials said the exercise is structured to progress in stages, beginning with subject-matter expert exchanges and command post drills before moving to situational training lanes and, ultimately, complex live-fire scenarios. This allows established procedures to be tested under increasingly demanding conditions.The exercise reflects Yudh Abhyas 2026's broader emphasis on integrated, multi-domain operations and is scheduled to continue until the end of September.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
articles.summary: The local authorities reportedly seize Tigray's airports following reports of recent drone strikes.
articles.body:
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.

Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.

Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.

The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.

It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.

Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance

"It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media.

The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.

Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.

Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.

This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.

On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.

The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.

"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.

Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.

He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.

But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.

The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.

On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.

It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.

Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.

It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.

Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.

In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.

Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.

There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

articles.title: How the 'Squatter Hunter' is fighting home takeovers with tech
articles.summary: Flash Shelton reveals how home security cameras and alarm systems can stop squatters before they claim tenant rights in your vacant property.
articles.body: You leave a home empty while you travel, prepare it for sale or help an aging parent move. Then an unfamiliar car appears in the driveway. Someone gets inside. Before long, that person may even claim to have a lease. That kind of situation turned Flash Shelton into the man now known as the "Squatter Hunter." I recently sat down with Shelton on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to talk about how his unusual line of work began and what homeowners can do before an unwanted occupant settles in. He stars in A&E's "Squatters," which follows him and his team as they help property owners reclaim homes from unauthorized occupants. What stood out during our conversation was how often his advice came back to technology. A camera alert or alarm can give you something that becomes much harder to get later: evidence of when someone showed up and how they got inside. NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com. Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward. HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY How protecting his mom created the 'Squatter Hunter' Shelton says none of this started as a business idea. After his father died in 2019, he moved his mother in with him while preparing her vacant home for sale. Then seven people took over the property. Shelton told me he was "just being a good son" and felt he had to protect his mother after the squatters took advantage of the empty house. He called the sheriff and says he was told there was little law enforcement could do because the situation had become a civil issue. Shelton knew almost nothing about squatting at the time, but he did not accept that answer. "I was like, screw that. I'm going to do something about it," he recalled. He started researching how squatters operate and when occupancy claims can become harder to untangle. His approach was unconventional. His mother, who owned the house, signed a legitimate lease giving Shelton the right to occupy the property. Shelton says he wanted documentation showing he had permission to be there in case the squatters produced a fake lease of their own. He then waited for the occupants to leave and entered the house using his key. Once inside, he started installing cameras and a security system. His thinking, he said, was that "if they can take a house, I can take a house." When some of the occupants returned, Shelton told them he had possession of the property and gave them until the end of the day to remove their furniture. He says cars and trucks soon arrived, and the house was cleared. Years later, that experience has turned into a full-time mission and an A&E series. Why squatting is getting more attention across the US Squatting can create a serious and expensive problem for homeowners, even though there is no reliable nationwide count showing exactly how often it happens. Part of the challenge is how these cases are tracked. Squatting does not appear as its own category in national crime databases, and cases can be handled differently depending on whether authorities view them as trespassing, fraud or a landlord-tenant dispute. That makes it difficult to put one national number on the problem. What we do know is that lawmakers across the country have been responding. As of July 2026, the National Apartment Association reported that 28 states had enacted laws addressing squatting. Another 25 states have introduced or considered legislation during 2026. Those measures include faster removal procedures and new penalties for some forms of unauthorized occupancy. There are also documented cases showing how disruptive squatting can become. A New York City Department of Investigation review found unauthorized occupants in 548 vacant NYCHA apartments. Joint DOI and NYPD operations reclaimed 60 of those apartments and resulted in 81 arrests involving unauthorized occupants accused of criminal activity connected with the properties. So while there is no single number showing how many homes are affected nationwide, the growing legislative response and documented cases make one thing clear: unauthorized home takeovers are a real problem, and homeowners have good reason to think about prevention before a property sits empty. LAKE TAHOE SQUATTER SUSPECT CAUGHT ON SURVEILLANCE IN RICH-AND-FAMOUS MOUNTAIN RETREAT The technology lesson Flash wishes he had learned sooner For all the unusual tactics Shelton has used since becoming the "Squatter Hunter," his biggest piece of advice is surprisingly simple. Put cameras on a vacant property before there is a problem. Looking back at his mother's home, Shelton told me, "If I had cameras on my mom's house back then, I wouldn't be the squatter hunter today." The back door had been broken. What Shelton lacked was proof showing exactly when the entry happened and who did it. He believes footage could have changed the situation from the beginning. With cameras, Shelton said, he could have shown authorities, "on this date, at this time, and this is the person." That is where today's home technology can make a real difference. A connected camera can alert you when somebody approaches a house. It can record an entry. It can also give law enforcement a timeline before competing stories about who belongs there begin. Why a fake lease can complicate everything One of the biggest challenges can appear after someone gets inside. Shelton says experienced squatters may produce a lease and claim they were given permission to live there. "They know that if they get into a property and show a lease and create reasonable doubt," Shelton told me, law enforcement may refer the property owner to the courts instead of immediately removing the occupant. That is another reason camera footage can become so useful. A document may say one thing. Video showing someone forcing a door or entering a clearly vacant home can provide additional evidence about what actually happened. Shelton says many of the people he encounters understand how housing rules work and try to use tenant protections to delay removal. Shelton says the goal is tenant rights, not adverse possession You hear the phrase "squatters' rights" constantly, but it can blur together very different legal concepts. Adverse possession generally requires someone to occupy property openly for a period set by state law while meeting other specific requirements. That can take years. Shelton says the disputes he deals with tend to revolve around something much more immediate: whether an unauthorized occupant can create enough uncertainty to be treated as a tenant. "Squatters are doing everything they can to gain tenant rights," Shelton told me. "They're not interested in squatter laws or rights. They want tenant rights." That helps explain why the legal response varies so much by state. Some states have created faster procedures for owners who say an unauthorized person took over a property. Others have increased penalties for fake leases or fraudulent documents. ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS Some cases go far beyond an empty vacation home Shelton has dealt with situations that sound much more disturbing than somebody slipping into an abandoned property. During our interview, he described a case involving an 88-year-old woman in Culver City, California, who had hired a caregiver. According to Shelton, the caregiver lost the job but refused to leave the home. He said the situation eventually required intervention through social services and described it as a case involving elder abuse. That experience sticks with him because the homeowner was especially vulnerable. Shelton has also worked on expensive properties. He recalled one Malibu home worth roughly $8 million and another case involving a Hollywood Hills mansion. His point was that there is no single profile of a property that can attract an unauthorized occupant. The same goes for the people involved. "They don't have a look," Shelton told me. "Squatters are your neighbors." Be careful before trying the Squatter Hunter approach yourself Watching Shelton confront people makes compelling television. Copying what you see on A&E could put you in a dangerous situation. The laws governing trespassing, tenancy and removal vary by state. If you discover somebody inside your property, call law enforcement and document what you can safely. Save camera footage. Preserve records showing when the property became vacant. Keep documentation identifying anyone who had permission to be there. If someone claims to be a tenant, an attorney familiar with local property law can help determine the appropriate next move. Shelton brings years of experience into these encounters. He also has experience with de-escalation, which is another reminder that the confrontations you see on television come with risks. That is very different from a homeowner walking into a house alone and confronting a stranger. Flash Shelton ultimately wants to put himself out of business The growing attention around squatting has turned Shelton into a television personality and given him more cases than he can handle. But he says his long-term goal goes in the opposite direction. "There are no shortage of cases" where people need help, he told me. Still, Shelton said, "I ultimately want to change these laws and put myself out of business." In the meantime, his biggest message for homeowners has less to do with dramatic confrontations. Pay attention early. A camera can tell you someone arrived. An alarm can tell you a door opened. A neighbor can tell you a moving truck has suddenly pulled into the driveway. Once somebody has spent time inside and starts claiming the right to be there, the situation can become much more complicated. NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE' Flash Shelton's tips to help protect your home from squatters During our conversation, I kept asking Shelton the question most homeowners probably have: What can I actually do before this happens? His advice focuses on making a vacant property easier to monitor while reducing the signs that nobody is around. 1) Put cameras around the property Start with cameras covering the most likely entry points. Shelton likes the fact that systems today allow homeowners to check their property remotely. As he told me, "you can be anywhere in the world" and monitor what is happening at home from your phone. Look for motion alerts and person detection. Night vision can help when someone arrives after dark. Also check how your recordings are stored. If an incident occurs, save important clips so they do not disappear when a cloud-storage retention period expires. You can see my picks for the 12 best outdoor security cameras at CyberGuy.com. 2) Make sure your security works when the power goes out A camera becomes a lot less useful if the electricity goes down. Shelton says he often works with battery-powered cameras because properties do not always have active power or internet access. Some batteries can keep a camera running for weeks or months, depending on the model and how frequently it records. He also recommends checking the backup capabilities of an alarm system. Before leaving a property vacant, Shelton told me to "make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date." That means testing the system before you leave instead of assuming last year's setup still works. For a more complete setup, see my Best Home Security Systems 2026 guide at CyberGuy.com. 3) Use lights to make the home appear occupied Shelton recommends timers for indoor lights and solar-powered security lighting when permanent power presents a problem. He also likes rechargeable lights with battery backup. That way, the house does not suddenly go completely dark during an outage. A smart plug or connected bulb can also let you adjust lighting remotely. The goal is to avoid broadcasting that a property has been sitting untouched. 4) Bring a trusted neighbor into the loop One of Shelton's most practical tips costs nothing. Tell trusted neighbors when a house will be vacant and make it clear whether anybody has permission to enter. As Shelton put it, "Your neighbors, they don't want you to have a squatter either." Ask them to contact you if an unfamiliar vehicle repeatedly appears in the driveway or someone begins carrying furniture inside. Shelton relied on a neighbor himself at his mother's house. The property had no Wi-Fi, so a neighbor allowed him to use a nearby connection for his camera. That option will depend on range and the equipment involved, but the larger lesson still works. A neighbor can notice activity before you ever receive a call from anyone else. 5) Secure your mailbox Shelton says people scouting vacant properties can pay attention to mailboxes. An overflowing box may signal that nobody has been around. He also worries about an unauthorized occupant receiving mail at an address and later presenting it as evidence that they live there. "Make sure you have a mailbox that is lockable," Shelton advised. If you are traveling, arrange to have your mail held or picked up. Also, pay attention if correspondence begins arriving for unfamiliar people at a property that should be empty. Our CyberGuy vacation guide has more on mail holds and home security before a trip: 6 things to do before you leave on vacation. 6) Ask about no-trespassing registration Putting up a no-trespassing sign sounds obvious. Shelton says homeowners should find out whether their local law enforcement agency offers an additional step. He told me that some sheriff's departments allow owners to file a form documenting that a property has been posted against trespassing. Why bother? A person can pull a sign down. Shelton described the thinking pretty simply: someone sees the notice, removes it and later says, "What sign?" Having something on file with local authorities may help document the owner's wishes even if the physical notice disappears. Procedures vary, so check directly with your local sheriff or police department before relying on this strategy. SAN FRANCISCO HOME WITH HISTORY OF SQUATTERS UNDER CONTRACT FOR $1.3 MILLION 7) Make an empty house look less empty Shelton also recommends thinking about the clues people can see from the street. Put lights on timers. Keep the yard maintained. Avoid leaving packages outside. If practical, Shelton suggests leaving a vehicle in the driveway. He even recommends asking a trusted friend whether they can park there while you are away. None of that guarantees somebody will stay away. It can make a vacant property less obvious to a person scouting for an easy target. 8) Check everything before leaving for vacation If you plan to be gone for a week or longer, Shelton recommends doing one final security check before you leave. "Make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date," he told me. Check camera batteries. Make sure motion alerts reach your phone. Confirm that your alarm is communicating properly. Also think about what happens if someone cuts the power or the neighborhood has an outage. Shelton recommends equipment with battery backup whenever possible. A few minutes spent testing everything before you leave could prevent you from discovering later that the camera you were counting on stopped recording days earlier. 9) Watch your home title too A squatter moving into a property does not automatically gain legal ownership of it. However, homeowners should also be aware of a separate threat called home title fraud. Criminals can use fraudulent documents or stolen personal information to try to change property records or obtain financing tied to a home. That makes property-record monitoring another layer of protection. A home title monitoring service can alert you to certain changes involving your property records, including a new owner, new lender or changes in financing. Home title monitoring cannot stop someone from entering your property or prevent a fraudulent filing. However, an alert can help you spot an unexpected change and investigate it sooner. See my tips and best picks on home title monitoring services at CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways What happened at Flash Shelton's mother's house shows how quickly a vacant property can become somebody else's opportunity. For me, the most useful part of his story comes before any confrontation. Shelton wishes he had cameras running when people first entered his mother's home. That says a lot. The sooner you know somebody has entered your property, the sooner you can call for help and preserve evidence showing what happened. I also would not overlook the low-tech advice. Tell a trusted neighbor when a property should be empty. Pay attention to the mailbox. Find out what your local police or sheriff recommends before you need them. And remember that the law is changing quickly. With 28 states now having enacted measures addressing squatting, you should check the rules where your property is located rather than assuming something you saw online applies everywhere. articles.title: Thames tunnel plan to heat 650,000 homes gets £41m funding boost
articles.summary: A new pipeline along the Thames will use heat from industry and redistribute it to homes across London.
articles.body:
A heat network that will run under and alongside the River Thames, using recycled heat to warm 650,000 homes in London, has been awarded £41m in government funding.

The London Strategic Heat Main will use excess heat from sources like data centres or factories, and transport it via a system of hot water pipes.

The initial phase will cross seven boroughs from Bexley in south London, through Greenwich, Lewisham, Southwark, City of London, Lambeth, and Westminster.

The funding comes as part of a wider £90 million investment by government into heat networks in London.

Heating homes currently contributes to about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, the government has reported .

The plan, which is already under development but subject to planning, could then be extended across Barking, Dagenham and Tower Hamlets in east London and Kensington and Chelsea in the west.

Eventually, a specially constructed tunnel beside and underneath the River Thames will carry hot water across the capital, and will circulate heat through homes and businesses along the route.

While the tunnel is being built, the project aims to transport hot water 15.5 miles (25km) each day using electric barges down the river instead.

Ministers say the project will help unlock about £5bn of investment in London's heat networks and support skilled jobs in tunnelling, engineering and river transport.

The pontoons storing the water tanks could also be developed into "Thames Floating Gardens", with the potential to create new green spaces similar to the embankments built in the 19th century to cover the London Underground.

£11.5m for a separate heat network development in Bexley and Greenwich, south-east London, which will serve up to 100,000 homes when fully built

£11.4m for a heat system in the Marble Arch area that will use water-source heat pumps to take energy from the London chalk aquifer - a large underground layer of chalk rock that stores and transmits rainwater - to heat offices, homes, hotels and businesses around Oxford Street.

£5.5m to upgrade the systems serving 1,143 residents at Prospect House in Bermondsey, south London, and the Packington Estate heat network in Islington, north London.

Energy minister Martin McCluskey said: "Clean power and clean heat benefit communities across our country.

"Building the infrastructure to deliver it is reindustrialising the UK and rolling out cutting-edge energy technology so families can benefit from lower bills, good jobs and energy security.

"For those already using heat networks, we are upgrading inefficient systems to make sure people get the high-quality, low-cost, reliable heating they deserve."

It is thought the project could be completed by the early 2030s.
