articles.title: Republicans may have gerrymandered their way into a Texas-sized Latino problem
articles.summary: (Corrects Trump's approval rating in paragraph three) By David Hood-Nuño and Evan Garcia DONNA, Texas, Sept 23 (Reuters) - South Texas unfurls in long stretc...
articles.body:
Republicans may have gerrymandered their way into a Texas-sized Latino problem

(Corrects Trump's approval rating in paragraph three)

DONNA, Texas, Sept 23 (Reuters) - South Texas unfurls in long stretches of highways across flat landscapes dotted with pump jacks, mesquite trees, and gas stations sporting prices that voters swear should not be this high. This territory swung heavily to Donald Trump in 2024 — but may shift again in 2026.

From the outskirts of San Antonio, through historic, sprawling ranchlands to the border city of McAllen, Reuters traveled more than 360 miles (580 km) and ‌spoke to more than 30 Latino voters, who shared a similar refrain: as President, Trump had a chance to lower prices across this expanse, where trucks and beef barbacoa are king, and failed.

Many are no longer convinced the Republican Party is looking out for people like ‌them. Frustration over economic pressures and Trump's immigration agenda is rising, exposing cracks in what Republican officials hoped was a durable political realignment among Latino Americans. Trump's approval rating nationwide has fallen to 32%, the lowest since returning to office, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

That uncertainty poses a problem for Texas Republicans, who redrew congressional maps last year betting the Latino ​contingent who helped power Trump's 2024 win would remain in their column.

Now, they're grappling with whether this notoriously swingy voting group may snap back to Democrats in the Lone Star State as they have in other parts of the country in off-year and special elections, said David Wasserman, elections analyst at the nonpartisan forecaster Cook Political Report.

Texas Republicans sought to make several districts more favorable to their candidates ahead of the 2026 elections, basing their changes on Trump's 2024 performance, the strongest showing among Latino voters by a Republican presidential candidate this century. Rather than dilute Latino voting power, many of the newly configured districts remained heavily Latino, including Texas' 15th and 35th Congressional Districts.

In District 15, Latinos account for 74.5% of the citizen voting-age population. In District 35, they make up 51.6%, according to the state's redistricting analysis. Yet both districts have become more competitive, with political prognostication site Sabato's Crystal Ball rating the 15th District a Toss-up and the 35th District Lean Republican. ‌Cook Political rates the 15th Lean Republican.

An August 2026 Texas Southern University poll found Democratic congressional candidates leading ⁠in three South Texas districts, including the 15th. Interviews with almost 50 analysts, activists, pollsters and voters back up the idea that some Latinos in South Texas who voted for Trump appear open to Democrats.

One of those is Saúl Guajardo, 53, of McAllen, who voted for Trump three times.

"I used to be a conservative, far-right," he said. "I'm more open than ever before to vote Democrat."

Guajardo said he and his wife Terrie live paycheck-to-paycheck, despite steady incomes. Gasoline is a big ⁠weight, as the average price of a gallon was $4.09 in the McAllen area as of September 22, according to AAA data.

Terrie said Trump's strict immigration enforcement "crackdown" was too harsh for people who simply want to work in the United States, as his policies have permanently separated some families trying to make a life in the U.S.

Polling suggests many Latinos are souring on Republicans. A September poll of 1,000 Latinos in Texas conducted for Cook Political and TelevisaUnivision found that 18% of Latinos who voted for Trump no longer support him, and almost two-thirds of Latino voters would be less likely to vote for candidates who support Trump's immigration policies.

For both parties, those shifts explain both ​the ​promise and peril of Latino voters. Their support has often proved less dependent on party loyalty than on whether they believe elected officials will improve their economic circumstances.

"It's not ​one of these that you're talking to a wall because they're all going to vote Democrat or they're all ‌going to vote Republican," said Daniel Alegre, CEO of Spanish-language media company TelevisaUnivision. "They're all going to vote for the person who is going to make their lives better."

Republicans reject the premise that Latino voters are moving away from them. Christian Martinez, the National Republican Congressional Committee's national Hispanic press secretary, said Democrats spent years responding to declining support among Hispanic voters with "denial, excuses, and condescension," instead of addressing concerns that drove many working-class voters toward Republicans.

The risk that redistricting backfires is particularly clear in the 15th District, which in its reconfigured form would have given Trump an 18-point win in 2024, compared with a two-point margin in 2020 and a 14-point loss in his first election in 2016.

That district's incumbent, Republican Monica De La Cruz, is facing a unique opponent in Democratic singer Bobby Pulido, whose celebrity status predates his entry into politics. His signature hit, "Desvelado," has nearly 610 million Spotify streams, and he has won two Latin Grammy Awards.

His economic message and crossover appeal have turned the district into one of the state's most closely watched races. A late August Texas Southern University poll had Pulido leading De La Cruz by five percentage points.

Dressed in a cowboy hat, blue jeans and cowboy boots, Pulido crisscrosses South Texas ‌on weekends, hopping from one quinceañera, a traditional 15th birthday celebration for girls in Latino communities, to another. His surprise — and free — appearances often end with a gift for ​the celebrant: a white hat with pink lettering reading "Make Quinceañeras Great Again."

Pulido said Democrats lost ground with Latino voters in South Texas because they failed to address the economic concerns ​that matter most to working families, though he said both major parties often misread the electorate.

"As a Democrat, I think that we misunderstand ​the Hispanic vote and I think, honestly, I think Republicans don't get it either," Pulido told Reuters. "We don't want handouts, we're very proud. We just want an opportunity to go work and make something and provide for our families, and then ‌work towards our kids prospering better than we did."

On August 1, Pulido surprised Melody Silva and roughly 200 ​relatives and friends gathered for her quinceañera. They screamed when he appeared at the ​top of a staircase and cheered louder when he mentioned his congressional race.

"He's got such great roots here in the Valley," said Michael Silva, Melody's father and a police officer in McAllen. "I feel like he's not just representing the Valley, but representing the raza, you know, the people, for us — locals."

His name recognition appears to be one of his greatest strengths. Among the dozen voters Reuters spoke to at a monthly outdoor market roughly 180 miles (290 km) north in rural Beeville, Pulido's name was as ubiquitous as the summer heat.

De La Cruz's campaign ​did not respond to requests for comment.

Ramon Barrera, 36, known as "The Texas Tea Guy" on social media, sees ‌the shift in sentiment. He posts short TikTok updates "spilling the tea" about politics and community issues, crisscrossing South Texas in his Dodge Ram 3500 to talk to locals, along with hunting for old furniture to refurbish.

He voted for Trump for the first time ​in 2024, describing himself as conservative but not strongly aligned with either party. He said Trump's term has been a disappointment, opening the door for him to vote for Pulido and Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor against Republican Greg Abbott, who is ​seeking a fourth consecutive term.

"The S&P 500 looks great, but our wallets don't," he said.

(Reporting by David Hood-Nuño; Editing by Kat Stafford and David Gaffen)

articles.title: 'Unwarranted': India rejects OIC's Kashmir references, slams outfit for giving platform to Pakistan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday hit back at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) over references to Jammu and Kashmir in a joint communique of its
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday hit back at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) over references to Jammu and Kashmir in a joint communique of its Contact Group, calling them “unwarranted and factually incorrect” and asserting that the grouping has no locus standi to comment on matters that are strictly internal to India.The ministry of external affairs said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are an “integral and inalienable part of India”, adding that “no amount of repetition of politically motivated propaganda can change this reality”.The response came after Pakistan’s foreign ministry said on X that deputy prime minister and foreign minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar had addressed a ministerial meeting of the OIC Contact Group on Jammu and Kashmir on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.According to Pakistan, Dar urged OIC member states to maintain a “unified position” on Jammu and Kashmir at the United Nations and other international fora. He also reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to a “just and peaceful settlement of the dispute in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the wishes of the Kashmiri people”.The references to Jammu and Kashmir drew a strong response from New Delhi.“India categorically rejects the unwarranted and factually incorrect references to India in the Joint Communique of the so-called OIC Contact Group on Jammu & Kashmir. The OIC has no locus standi to pronounce on matters that are strictly internal to India,” the MEA said in a statement.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal shared the statement on X, reiterating India’s position on the OIC communique.The ministry also questioned the credibility of the grouping over its repeated backing of what it described as politically motivated narratives.“Repeated endorsement of such motivated narratives only raises serious questions on the credibility of OIC,” the MEA said.India further turned its focus on Pakistan, saying the OIC should address terrorism emanating from Pakistani territory instead of providing Islamabad a platform for what New Delhi called “fabricated and motivated propaganda”.“Instead of offering a platform to Pakistan to peddle its fabricated and motivated propaganda, OIC will be better advised to counsel Pakistan, which has a well-documented record of supporting and sponsoring terrorism, to look inwards and address the continuing threat of terrorism emanating from territories under its control,” the MEA said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades
articles.summary: Residents on North Ronaldsay toasted the birth of Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford with a dram of whisky last week.
articles.body:
A baby has been born on Orkney's most northerly island for the first time in more than three decades.

Parents Jorge Suarez and Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week.

Islanders toasted the birth with a dram of whisky to celebrate the first newborn in the remote location since Thomas Brookman in August 1992.

The family, who split their time between Costa Rica and Orkney and travelled more than 5,000 miles for the birth, said Duncan was born in a much-loved place.

"North Ronaldsay has always been a very special place for me and I felt alive and free here every summer when I came up as a little girl," Alice told BBC Scotland News.

"My intuition was telling me this was the right place for us so we spoke to the NHS to see if it would be possible.

"We have this beautiful family home steeped in our history and ancestry so to be surrounded by that felt a very special introduction for him to come to Earth."

North Ronaldsay is Orkney's northernmost island and is only accessible from Kirkwall on the main island via a 20-minute plane journey or a ferry, which takes two hours and 40 minutes.

The island is famous for its seaweed-eating sheep, which are mostly confined to the shore by a 13-mile-long drystone wall that encircles the island.

Baby Duncan was born in Holland House, which was built by Alice's ancestors - the Traill family - who bought the island in 1727.

The house has been passed down through generations and is still owned by her family.

Alice's grandfather, Duncan, was the former Laird of North Ronaldsay and provided the inspiration for her son's name.

"I didn't know I was going to name him after Duncan when we arrived but I was sitting on the sofa and right in front of me was a collage of his pictures with my grandmother, so he has been very present with us," Alice said.

"He was an incredible man, very kind and really strong and I felt like there would be no better name than his to carry on and continue his legacy in the world."

Historically when the Laird was on the island, a flag was flown at Holland House to inform the residents.

So when baby Duncan was born at 04:05 on 15 September, Alice and Jorge followed the tradition to share the news.

"Over the years we have found a lot of magical four-leaf clovers here and have kept them in a book," Alice said.

"We stuck a four-leaf clover to a glass bottle, glued a Groatie Buckie to the lid then filled it with whisky and gave it to each of the islanders.

"We raised the flag and everybody opened their whisky and shared a dram - a celebratory drink - together."

A Groatie Buckie is a small, pale pink and white shell found on beaches across Orkney, which in local tradition brings good luck and fortune to the keeper.

The family will return to Costa Rica in November, where the couple run a school.

But Alice is certain her children will have the same opportunity to spend time in North Ronaldsay as she did growing up.

"Duncan will absolutely be back every year," she said.

"One of the things I want to give my children is the gift my mother gave us, bringing us to this island every summer, letting us run wild, explore the island and feel the connection to the community."

articles.title: Boston Globe op-ed says violence against transgender people is 'going down' despite activist claims
articles.summary: A Boston Globe opinion piece cited data from the Advocates for Trans Equality and the Human Rights Campaign showing a significant drop in violent transgender deaths.
articles.body: The Boston Globe published an opinion piece on Tuesday declaring that violence against transgender people was "going down" under President Donald Trump, contrary to warnings from transgender advocacy groups. The article, written by former USA Today columnist David Mastio, cited statistics from Advocates for Trans Equality and the Human Rights Campaign (HRC) that Mastio said showed substantial declines in recorded violent deaths in recent years. Despite this, Mastio noted that the organizations have continued warning about violence against transgender people. "Advocacy groups insist the data is incomplete and shouldn’t be used to draw any conclusions about the prevalence of anti-trans violence," Mastio wrote. "That’s due, they say, to the bigotry of families and authorities who misname and misgender the victims, making it hard to discern from public records how many transgender people are dying." MOTHER JONES' WNBA 'TRANS PANIC' STORY SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN ACTIVISM MASQUERADES AS JOURNALISM The article's headline read, "In Trump’s America, violence against transgender people isn’t going up — it’s going down." He continued, "Still it’s hard to imagine that as awareness about the transgender community has grown, misgendering and pronoun-swapping have become more common in police reports and news accounts than they were a decade ago, when another prominent LGBTQ organization, the Human Rights Campaign, began publishing its own numbers on violence against transgender people. The HRC tallies, too, find a declining number of violent transgender deaths to mourn. The group found a peak in 2021 of 47 deaths falling to 27 last year. HRC described that 40 percent drop as an 'ongoing onslaught of violence.'" Mastio wrote, "But despite a hostile Trump administration and a barrage of anti-trans legislation across the country, the number of violent deaths the group documents has fallen nearly 50 percent from 53 in 2023 to 27 in 2025." Mastio also cited a report from the Manhattan Institute, which asserted that the transgender population actually has a lower murder rate than the population as a whole. He added that the HRC did not respond to a request for comment when asked to rebut the report. The report was written by Vincent Lundgren and Manhattan Institute fellow Colin Wright. Fox News Digital reached out to the HRC for comment. The Advocates for Trans Equality told Fox News Digital that a "dip in one datapoint" does not suggest that transgender people are any safer today. DOUG SCHOEN: WHY DEMOCRATS CANNOT BREAK FREE FROM THE FAR LEFT’S TRANSGENDER DEMANDS "Anyone claiming trans people are safer today under the Trump administration is ignoring what’s happening. Right now, everyone in this country, trans people included, is facing Medicaid cuts, soaring gas prices, ICE terrorizing our communities, and attacks on the right to vote. On top of that, attacks on trans people have been relentless," the organization said. It continued, "This year alone, lawmakers across the country introduced over 700 anti-trans bills. Trans people are being cut off from gender-affirming care, denied IDs that match who they are, and housed in prisons that don’t match their gender. Any one of these makes trans people less safe. Together, they are a deliberate, hateful attack on the trans community under this administration, and people will die because of it." Manhattan Institute fellow Colin Wright called the Globe column a "shockingly sober article" that cited his report and said he was not surprised the HRC did not respond to Mastio. PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME "That's unsurprising because the HRC is engaging in fundraising propaganda. They don't care about the truth, only promoting the narrative. Our report presenting the actual data is irrefutable. That's why they have nothing to say in response," Wright wrote on X. In comments to Fox News Digital, Wright said he was glad to see a mainstream outlet report on his data and hoped the article marked a turning point for the media. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I do hope this is a sign that the media is no longer being held hostage by activists and is slowly being allowed to think again. At the Manhattan Institute, we believe that real justice requires an unwavering commitment to the truth. We have presented that truth in our report, and now the media must decide whether to acknowledge it or hide from it," Wright said. The Boston Globe told Fox News Digital in a statement, "This is a guest op-ed. The views expressed in the piece are those of the author. Globe Opinion publishes a wide range of viewpoints and perspectives."

articles.title: New Jersey police pull out 3-foot python from woman's car grille, bodycam video shows
articles.summary: Body camera footage shows New Jersey police dismantling a car's front bumper to free a 3-foot ball python wedged inside the vehicle's grille.
articles.body: A New Jersey woman got a slithery surprise when she returned home from a wheel alignment and discovered a 3-foot python wedged inside the front grille of her car — prompting police to dismantle part of the vehicle to free the reptile. Aiyana Hudson made the startling discovery on Sept. 14 in Franklin Township and called police for help, according to WABC-TV. Body camera footage showed responding officers inspecting the car and working to determine how to safely remove the snake. Officer Lisseth Villacis told the outlet that police initially contacted animal control but were told the agency only handled domesticated animals. SURPRISE TRAVELER TRAPPED BENEATH CAR FOR HUNDREDS OF MILES GETS NEW CHANCE AT LIFE "We tried getting animal control out there, and they're like, they only deal with domesticated animals," Villacis said. "And we're like, oh shoot. OK. So, we're kind of like the last resort." Officers then took matters into their own hands, removing parts of the vehicle, including the front bumper, to reach the trapped reptile, as seen in the footage. After about 20 minutes, police managed to untangle and safely free the snake, which animal control officials identified as a 3-foot ball python. HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL PLAYER PRACTICES WITH VENOMOUS SNAKE HIDING INSIDE HELMET BEFORE COACH'S DISCOVERY Hudson said she was relieved the unexpected passenger never found its way inside the vehicle while she was in it. "I was just really happy that it didn't, like, pop its head through the AC vent when I was driving or come in through the steering wheel," Hudson told the outlet. "I want to let you know my car would have been lit on fire, and we'd be calling the fire department at that point." How the python ended up in the grille remains unclear. The snake was unharmed and taken to the Franklin Township Animal Shelter, according to MyCentralJersey.com. Residents who have pet snakes and can no longer care for them should surrender it to the township animal shelter, he said.

articles.title: Florida town told employees their pensions had moved to the state system; 5 months later, a paperwork error revealed they were never enrolled
articles.summary: For nearly five months, employees of Lake Park, Florida, had no way to confirm whether roughly $60,000 a month in pension contributions, 3% of their pay
articles.body: For nearly five months, employees of Lake Park, Florida, had no way to confirm whether roughly $60,000 a month in pension contributions, 3% of their pay plus a 14% town match, was actually being invested, according to WLRN NPR News. The town had told workers its pension migration to the Florida Retirement System took effect on 1 July 2025, but two administrators failed to submit key paperwork and never spoke to resolve it, leaving the town unenrolled in FRS entirely.How Lake Park's pension migration went wrongThe town was meant to complete its move from a Corebridge Financial-administered pension to the Florida Retirement System by 1 July 2025. On 24 April 2025, FRS bureau chief Hobart Lawrance emailed both Finance Director Barbara Gould and then-Assistant Town Manager Bambi McKibbon-Turner, telling them the town still needed to send employee information along with four required documents to complete the enrollment. A follow-up reminder went unanswered in June, and on 16 June, just two weeks before the enrollment was due to go live, McKibbon-Turner forwarded the email to Gould asking how she could help. The two never spoke about it, and the paperwork was never submitted.Employees' months of unanswered questionsBelieving they were enrolled, employees soon found they couldn't access their accounts online and began emailing Gould directly, questions that never reached Reade. In August, one worker asked where to elect their FRS plan; Gould told them to wait for a welcome packet. By September, an employee reported being told by FRS that she wasn't in the system at all. In October, another employee contacted FRS directly and was told they do not see the town of Lake Park as an active participant in the plan at all, a claim confirmed by a senior FRS team member, according to WLRN.The whistleblower who pushed for an investigationLaura Mochi, a cashier in the Finance Department who had watched employees' concerns go unaddressed, called FRS Director Kathy Gould in late October to tell her the town had been collecting pension payments without ever formally joining FRS. Kathy Gould referred the matter to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, and an FDLE investigator later reached Barbara Gould on 3 November. That same week, Mochi filed a report with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and, on 5 November, submitted a complaint to the Palm Beach County Inspector General's Office, backed by emails documenting the missed communications.Town manager Rich Reade's response and the ongoing inspector general probeReade said he only learned of the problem on 5 November, after which he completed the outstanding paperwork himself in roughly 10 to 15 minutes, retroactively enrolling the town in FRS effective 1 December, backdated to 1 July. He suspended Gould for three days in December for “concealing defective work,” while placing responsibility on McKibbon-Turner, who had overseen the transition before resigning on 31 July. Reade told commissioners in November that no financial penalty applied, though the town would need to cover employees' lost investment earnings, an amount the town is still calculating through a separate actuarial report tied to a union grievance, while the Inspector General's investigation into the broader episode also remains unfinished.You use AI every day. articles.body:
Police are investigating the death of a man following an assault in Ballymena in the early hours of Saturday morning.

Christopher Houston, also known as Cricki, was found unconscious at the junction of Alexander Street and Broughshane Street just after 05:00 BST on 19 September. He died in hospital on Tuesday night.

Police said the 42-year-old had been the victim of an assault and sustained a head injury.

A 39-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm on Saturday and subsequently released on bail to allow for further police enquiries.

Police are appealing to anyone with information to come forward.

articles.title: Pakistan’s hidden health crisis: Children contract HIV after routine hospital care
articles.summary: A routine visit to a hospital has turned into a life-changing ordeal for dozens of families in Pakistan, with parents alleging that their children
articles.body: A routine visit to a hospital has turned into a life-changing ordeal for dozens of families in Pakistan, with parents alleging that their children contracted HIV while receiving medical care.The children were reportedly being treated for ordinary illnesses or undergoing routine procedures when, weeks or months later, they were found to be HIV positive, according to NPR. Their families say they had no other known explanation for how the children could have contracted the virus.Parents interviewed by NPR have pointed to poor infection-control practices at healthcare facilities, particularly the alleged reuse of syringes and needles during injections and intravenous (IV) treatment. They believe such practices may have exposed their children to HIV.The reported cases have brought devastating consequences for affected families. At least six children have died, while others face a lifetime of treatment and medical monitoring after being diagnosed with the virus.HIV weakens the immune system and currently has no cure, but antiretroviral treatment can control the virus and help people live longer, healthier lives. For families in the affected communities, however, the diagnosis has brought additional financial and social pressures, including the cost of medicines and repeated hospital visits and fears of stigma.Many parents are now seeking answers from the healthcare system. They want authorities to investigate how children with no apparent risk factors came to be infected and whether lapses in basic medical safety standards played a role.The allegations have also put a spotlight on infection-control practices at some Pakistani healthcare facilities. Families and rights advocates are calling for investigations, greater monitoring of hospitals and stricter safeguards around the use of medical equipment.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, a woman paid $4 for a thrift-store painting; experts authenticated it as an N.C. Wyeth work; after a $191,000 auction fell through; then it sold privately for over $100,000
articles.summary: Every thrifter dreams of it: buying something for less than a pizza, discovering it's actually valuable, and walking away with a fortune.
articles.body: Every thrifter dreams of it: buying something for less than a pizza, discovering it's actually valuable, and walking away with a fortune. For Tracy Donahue, a New Hampshire resident, the dream happened to be real.In 2017, she picked up a painting at a thrift store for $4. She hung it in her bedroom and forgot about it. Six years later, she'd find out it was a genuine N.C. Wyeth, one of the most celebrated American illustrators of the 20th century. By fall 2023, it was heading to auction with a $150,000 to $250,000 estimate. The winning bid came in at $191,000. Weeks passed. The sale was eventually cancelled. Donahue had already planned what she would do with the money. She and her family had hoped to use the proceeds to visit their son in Germany. But the buyer vanished. Just when Donahue was beginning to lose hope, a private collector showed up and bought the painting for more than $100,000.The rare find at SaversIn 2017, Tracy Donahue walked into a Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. She was hunting for picture frames when she spotted it: a dusty oil painting wedged among discarded posters at the store. The painting spoke to her. She was curious about the women. Who are they? Why are they so tense? And the only answer she had was: this painting is coming home. After all, it only cost $4. She paid the money and clunked it into the cart. She had no idea she was wheeling out an oil panel by N.C. Wyeth, who is known for works including ‘Treasure Island’, ‘Robin Hood’ and ‘Robinson Crusoe’. The store, too, wasn’t aware of its value. “We look at all the donations we receive, and we place a value on them as best we can,” Savers manager Shaun Edson told the New York Times later. “We are not connoisseurs of paintings. We do our best to evaluate the pieces and value them appropriately.” And just like that, Donahue took home the long-lost work of the artist for less than the price of a drink.She discovers what she really boughtTracy Donahue hung the painting in her bedroom for years, and then eventually stored it in a closet, according to a report by CNN. She never would have known without spring cleaning. In May 2023, while tidying her home, she spotted the painting again and noticed something: a signature label on the back. She posted a photo to a Facebook group called ‘Things Found in Walls’, which is dedicated to “stories of things you have found in walls, dug up in your backyard, or in that abandoned house across the street from your grandma’s,” according to the group’s description. She asked if anyone knew anything about it. Within hours, her inbox filled with comments. This wasn't just old. This was valuable.Lauren Lewis, an art conservator, saw the post. She had worked with paintings by three generations of the Wyeths: N.C. Wyeth, his son Andrew Wyeth and his grandson Jamie Wyeth. Lewis reached out. She drove three hours to Donahue's home to examine the piece in person. After verification, Lewis was “99% certain it was authentic,” The Boston Globe reported. “While it certainly had some small scratches and it could use a surface clean, it was in remarkable condition considering none of us had any idea of its journey over the last 80 years.”That painting was a frontispiece illustration by N.C. Wyeth for the 1939 edition of Helen Hunt Jackson's Ramona. It featured two women: a young maiden and her rigid foster mother. The work was one of only four that Wyeth had created for that edition, and most of them had been lost to time.The auction and initial biddingBonhams Skinner announced it would go to auction in September 2023 with an estimate of $150,000 to $250,000. Wyeth's work, especially his book illustrations, has great value. His paintings have hung in major museums. His legacy has shaped American visual culture. So, the bidding began at $150,000. An Australian buyer placed the only bid, driving the price to $191,000 with the buyer's premium. Donahue was thrilled. She had plans for that money. She and her family wanted to use the money to visit their son in Germany, a trip they had been putting off for years. But then nothing happened. The potential buyer went silent. Bonhams Skinner cancelled the sale and returned the painting. Donahue called it her ‘biggest disappointment ever’. At the time, she also told reporters that she was relieved they hadn't spent money in advance, but the emotional letdown was real.A few months later, Aviva Lehmann, an auctioneer at Heritage Auctions, saw the news about the failed sale and immediately thought of a private collector she knew, someone serious enough and wealthy enough to care about owning a rare Wyeth. Lehmann called Donahue at 3 a.m. and fixed the sale, according to the Times. The painting was finally sold. The final price? Over $100,000. It’s certainly less than the failed auction, but more than what anyone expected from a $4 thrift-store find! More importantly, the money actually arrived. Donahue said goodbye to the painting, collected the money, called her son in Germany and informed him they were visiting.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: An Oklahoma homeowner who bought five acres of land from his grandfather in 1994 has learned that local authorities claim ownership of a narrow strip of land right next to his house, which is now set to be sold at a public tax auction. Thirty-two years after buying the rural property, the homeowner was told by Oklahoma County officials that a 40-foot strip of land just inches from his front door technically belongs to the county. Local authorities plan to put the disputed piece of land up for auction, with bidding set to start at $29,000. According to an investigation published by AOL News, the dispute centers on a long-standing boundary mistake that went unnoticed for more than three decades, despite multiple tax assessments and property reviews.A thirty-two-year land ownership surpriseThe homeowner originally bought the five-acre plot from his grandfather in 1994, believing the sale covered the full area around his family home. For 32 years, he mowed the yard, paid property taxes, and lived on the land without ever hearing about any boundary dispute from local government. The issue came up recently when Oklahoma County officials reviewed regional land records and found an unassigned, tax-delinquent strip measuring 40 feet wide right along his house. County records published online through DocketCity, which covers Oklahoma County public meetings, show that the land in question was flagged during a routine review of county-held property and unpaid tax rolls. The county then listed the narrow strip of land for public auction to recover unpaid taxes, setting a minimum opening bid of $29,000.Structural proximity and access concernsThe planned sale creates major problems for the homeowner because of exactly where the 40-foot strip sits. Since the marked boundary runs within inches of his home's foundation, a sale to an outside buyer at auction could seriously limit access to his house, driveway, and utilities. Under local zoning and land use rules, selling the strip to an outside bidder could create a legal conflict over access rights, possibly leaving the homeowner without clear rights to reach parts of his own home. Reporting by AOL News noted that the homeowner has tried to negotiate directly with Oklahoma County commissioners and county assessors to fix the administrative error or remove the land from the upcoming auction before bidding starts.Public meetings and local government responseThe land dispute was placed on the official agenda during Oklahoma County commission meetings, where officials discussed the legal status of county-acquired property and tax sale procedures. According to meeting minutes available on DocketCity, county boards must follow state legal rules when it comes to selling tax-delinquent properties. Once a property is formally certified for tax sale, removing it from the process often requires court involvement or clear approval from the board to pause the auction. Oklahoma County officials said tax sales are carried out strictly under state property laws to resolve long-standing ownership gaps and return unclaimed land to active tax rolls. The homeowner continues to seek a resolution with county officials or legal counsel to secure ownership of the 40-foot strip and stop the land from going up for auction.You use AI every day.
